events.title: Invasion of Poland
events.blurb: At 4:43 in the morning a warship opened fire on a peninsula garrison, and within minutes armoured columns and aircraft were crossing a national border along a 1,600-kilometre front from three directions simultaneously. Two days later, two of the invader's neighbours declared war — and the world's largest conflict had begun.
events.revealBlurb: September 1, 1939 — the battleship Schleswig-Holstein fired the first shots at Westerplatte. The 88-man garrison held out for seven days against a force many times its size. Poland was split between Germany and the Soviet Union by October 6; a government-in-exile continued the fight from London.

events.title: Scuttling of the Graf Spee
events.blurb: A feared commerce-raider that had sunk nine merchant ships in three months limped into a neutral harbour for repairs after a running battle with three smaller cruisers, then sat immobile while international diplomacy set a 72-hour countdown. Twenty thousand spectators lined the waterfront to watch her captain make his final decision.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1939, Montevideo. Captain Hans Langsdorff scuttled the Admiral Graf Spee at 8:55 PM rather than risk his crew in what he believed was an overwhelming British trap. Three days later he wrapped himself in the ship's battle ensign and shot himself. The trap was largely bluff.

events.title: Japanese-American Internment
events.blurb: A presidential order authorised the forced removal of all people of a specific ethnic ancestry from the entire western coast of a country — regardless of citizenship — to inland camps surrounded by guard towers and barbed wire, without trial or individual evidence of wrongdoing. Roughly 122,000 people were displaced; two-thirds were native-born citizens.
events.revealBlurb: Executive Order 9066, signed February 19, 1942. The Supreme Court upheld it in 1944. In 1988, Congress formally apologised and paid $20,000 in reparations to each surviving detainee — roughly 82,000 people. A 2011 Department of Justice memo officially acknowledged the government's lawyers had hidden evidence of innocence from the original court.

events.title: Warsaw Uprising
events.blurb: A resistance army launched an all-out urban insurrection timed to coincide with an approaching allied army's arrival at the city's eastern bank, intending to liberate the capital before that army entered — but the expected support never came, leaving 40,000 fighters and 200,000 civilians to a 63-day battle against overwhelming force that ended in total destruction.
events.revealBlurb: August 1 – October 2, 1944. The Polish Home Army rose at 5:00 PM on August 1 with roughly 40,000 fighters. The approaching Soviet Army halted on the opposite bank and waited. Stalin also denied Allied planes permission to use Soviet airfields for supply drops for weeks. An estimated 200,000 civilians were killed; survivors were expelled and the city was systematically demolished.

events.title: Japan's Formal Surrender
events.blurb: Aboard a battleship anchored in a bay surrounded by an Allied fleet of 250 ships, representatives of a defeated empire signed the instrument of its unconditional surrender on a folding table set up on the deck, ending the largest armed conflict in human history after six years of fighting across every ocean and every inhabited continent.
events.revealBlurb: September 2, 1945 — USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay. General MacArthur opened the ceremony: "We are gathered here to conclude a solemn agreement." The signing took 23 minutes. Japan's foreign minister, in top hat and tails, signed on behalf of the government. Allied Commander MacArthur used five pens to sign, giving them to survivors of Bataan, Corregidor, and others.

events.title: Faraday Demonstrates Induction
events.blurb: A 40-year-old self-taught English scientist, working in a London institution's basement, wrapped an iron ring with two coils of insulated wire, connected one coil to a battery and the other to a galvanometer, and observed that momentarily closing or opening the battery circuit caused a pulse of current in the other coil. The discovery — electromagnetic induction — was the foundation principle of every electrical generator and transformer ever built.
events.revealBlurb: August 29, 1831 — Michael Faraday at the Royal Institution. He had been a bookbinder's apprentice with barely any formal schooling; Humphry Davy hired him as a lab assistant and he eclipsed his mentor. He was offered a knighthood twice and the presidency of the Royal Society; he refused both.

events.title: Drake Strikes Oil
events.blurb: A former railroad conductor, working on behalf of a small Pennsylvania oil-extraction company, struck oil at a depth of 21 metres while drilling a well using salt-drilling techniques borrowed from Chinese craftsmen. The well produced about 25 barrels a day — at the time, world-altering. Within two years, western Pennsylvania had hundreds of wells; within twenty, American oil companies were exporting kerosene around the world; within fifty, petroleum had overtaken coal as the premier industrial fuel.
events.revealBlurb: August 27, 1859 — Edwin Drake at Titusville, Pennsylvania. Drake himself died poor; he had failed to patent his drilling-pipe innovations. John D. Rockefeller entered the Cleveland refining business five years later and, with Standard Oil, came to dominate the industry within a decade.

events.title: Edison's Practical Lightbulb
events.blurb: After 14 months of systematic experimentation with thousands of possible filament materials — and many previous lightbulb designs by other inventors — an American inventor's laboratory team achieved a 40-hour burn using a carbonized cotton-thread filament in an evacuated glass bulb. The achievement's significance was not inventing the lightbulb itself (which had existed in various forms for decades) but making one that burned long enough to be commercially viable.
events.revealBlurb: October 21, 1879 — Thomas Edison at Menlo Park. His 1880 improved version used a bamboo filament and burned 1,200 hours. Edison's real genius was less invention than the systematic industrial R&D lab he created — the template for every modern corporate research operation.

events.title: Brooklyn Bridge Opens
events.blurb: The longest suspension bridge in the world — 486 metres between its Gothic granite towers — opened to foot and carriage traffic linking Manhattan and Brooklyn across the East River. Its construction had taken 14 years and cost 27 lives. The chief engineer had been paralyzed by decompression sickness while supervising caisson work; his wife Emily had effectively managed the final decade of the project from notes dictated in his sickroom.
events.revealBlurb: May 24, 1883 — designed by John A. Roebling (who died from a dockside accident early in construction). His son Washington Roebling suffered caisson disease and was bedridden; daughter-in-law Emily Warren Roebling led onsite engineering management. She was the first person to cross the completed bridge, in a carriage carrying a rooster.

events.title: Wright Brothers' First Flight
events.blurb: Two American bicycle-shop owners from Dayton, Ohio achieved the first sustained, controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft on a windswept dune at the Outer Banks of North Carolina. The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 36 metres — about the wingspan of a modern commercial airliner. They made three more flights that morning; the fourth covered 260 metres in 59 seconds. Few newspapers reported the achievement; commercial aviation took another three decades to arrive.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1903 — Orville and Wilbur Wright at Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, NC. The flyer is now in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum. The pair spent 4 years after their first flight battling patent disputes and litigation rather than manufacturing planes.

events.title: Mosaic Browser Released
events.blurb: Undergraduate students at a University of Illinois supercomputing centre released a graphical web browser for Unix, with a version for Windows and Mac released later in the year. Unlike the earlier terminal-based browsers, it could display images inline with text. Within 18 months, web traffic had grown by 10,000 percent. The browser's lead developer would leave to co-found a company that would dominate the next phase.
events.revealBlurb: April 22, 1993 — developed at the NCSA, lead developer Marc Andreessen. Andreessen co-founded Netscape within a year. Mosaic was free for non-commercial use, a decision that gave the web the critical mass it needed.

events.title: eBay Founded
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Iranian-American software engineer set up an online auction site over the Labor Day weekend, initially as a hobby project on a personal server. One of the first items sold was a broken laser pointer for $14.83. When he emailed the buyer to check whether he understood it was broken, the buyer replied that he collected broken laser pointers. The founder realized he had a business on his hands.
events.revealBlurb: September 3, 1995 — Pierre Omidyar. He originally named it AuctionWeb; renamed eBay in 1997, short for Echo Bay Technology, his consulting firm. The first commission was sent as a personal check for $241.19.

events.title: Google Incorporated
events.blurb: Two Stanford PhD students filed articles of incorporation for a search-engine company they had been developing in a dormitory and a rented garage in suburban California. Their algorithm, unlike those of competitors, ranked pages by how many other pages linked to them. They would never graduate. Their search index contained 60 million pages when they incorporated; it contains hundreds of billions today.
events.revealBlurb: September 4, 1998 — Larry Page and Sergey Brin. The name is a misspelling of "googol," the mathematical term for 10^100. Their initial financial backer, Sun Microsystems co-founder Andy Bechtolsheim, wrote a $100,000 check to "Google Inc." before the company formally existed.

events.title: Wikipedia Launched
events.blurb: A 34-year-old internet entrepreneur who had been trying to build an online encyclopedia by paying credentialed experts to write and peer-review articles gave up on the slow model and switched to a radical alternative: a wiki, editable by anyone. The new version grew faster than expected. It had more articles in its first year than the slow-model version had produced in a previous eighteen months.
events.revealBlurb: January 15, 2001 — Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger. By 2007 Wikipedia had surpassed Britannica in size and approximately in accuracy. Today's English Wikipedia has over 6.9 million articles, and the full project runs in 340+ languages.

events.title: Reddit Founded
events.blurb: Two 22-year-old University of Virginia roommates who had just moved to Massachusetts on a Y Combinator fellowship launched a link-aggregation and discussion site that would, over the next two decades, become what its users called "the front page of the internet." The initial userbase was boosted by the founders themselves maintaining dozens of fake accounts to seed discussions. They sold the site to Condé Nast 16 months later for a reported $10-20 million.
events.revealBlurb: June 23, 2005 — Steve Huffman and Alexis Ohanian; later joined by Aaron Swartz, the open-internet activist who would die in 2013 facing federal prosecution. The site's iconic mascot, Snoo, was designed by Ohanian on a napkin.

events.title: Deposition of Romulus Augustulus
events.blurb: The Germanic warlord Odoacer deposed the sixteen-year-old emperor Romulus Augustulus at Ravenna — a boy whose mocking nickname meant "Little Augustus" — and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople, informing the eastern emperor that the west no longer needed a separate ruler. Odoacer spared Romulus's life, finding him too young and too minor to bother executing, and exiled him to a villa in Campania on a pension.
events.revealBlurb: September 4, 476 CE. The last western emperor's name combined the city's legendary founder and its first emperor — an irony Roman writers noticed immediately. Contemporaries did not regard this moment as "the fall of Rome"; that framing came centuries later. The eastern empire in Constantinople continued for another 977 years.

events.title: Charlemagne Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A Frankish king, in a papal basilica in the old western imperial capital for Christmas Mass, rose from prayer to be unexpectedly crowned "Emperor of the Romans" by the pope. The coronation resurrected, at least in title, a western empire that had been extinct for 324 years, and established a relationship between popes and emperors that would shape European politics for eight centuries.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 800 — Charlemagne in Rome, crowned by Pope Leo III. Charlemagne later claimed he had been surprised — but the pope probably wouldn't have dared without his consent. The Holy Roman Empire survived in one form or another until 1806.

events.title: Council of Clermont
events.blurb: The pope, addressing a crowd of French clergy and nobles in an open field outside a central French city after a church council, called on Christendom to take up arms and march east to recover a holy land from Muslim rule. "Deus vult," the crowd cried back — "God wills it." Within three years, 100,000 pilgrims and knights would be on the road.
events.revealBlurb: November 27, 1095 — Pope Urban II. His stated goals shifted in each retelling; the Byzantine emperor had only asked for mercenaries. The First Crusade's armies would surprise everyone, including themselves, by actually reaching Jerusalem.

events.title: Sack of Constantinople
events.blurb: A Crusader army that had set out to conquer Egypt, diverted by debts to a Venetian fleet and a pretender to the Byzantine throne, instead besieged the walls of the greatest Christian city in the world. They breached them, sacked the capital for three days, melted down ancient bronze statuary, and installed a Latin emperor. The Byzantine state never fully recovered.
events.revealBlurb: April 12-15, 1204 — the Fourth Crusade. The Venetians hauled the four bronze horses of the Hippodrome back to mount them above the entrance to St. Mark's Basilica, where reproductions stand today. Pope Innocent III was horrified and excommunicated the army — retroactively.

events.title: Marco Polo Departs for China
events.blurb: A 17-year-old Venetian merchant's son set out with his father and uncle on a journey across Asia to the court of the Mongol emperor. He would return to Venice 24 years later and, captured in a war with Genoa three years after that, dictate an account of his travels to a cellmate. The resulting book became the most influential western description of Asia for the next three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: 1271 — Marco left Venice with Niccolò and Maffeo Polo. Returning in 1295, he was imprisoned by the Genoese; his cellmate Rustichello da Pisa helped him write "Il Milione." Christopher Columbus's annotated copy survives.

events.title: First Human in Orbit
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Soviet Air Force pilot rode a modified intercontinental ballistic missile into a single orbit reaching 327 km altitude, completing one lap of Earth in 108 minutes before ejecting from his capsule at 7 km and parachuting separately to a field in southern Russia. The mission was fully automated; Gagarin held an emergency manual-control key sealed in an envelope in case he needed it.
events.revealBlurb: April 12, 1961 — Vostok 1. Gagarin was chosen partly because he was 1.57 m tall and fit the cramped capsule. He shouted "Poyekhali!" ("Let's go!") at liftoff — the same casual phrase Russian pilots use to start any flight. The module didn't fully separate and sent him spinning at 8 Gs before a wire bundle burned through.

events.title: First American in Space
events.blurb: Alan Shepard rode a Redstone rocket on a 15-minute suborbital arc reaching 187 km altitude, becoming the first American in space — 23 days after Yuri Gagarin's orbital flight. Unlike Gagarin's automated mission, Shepard manually controlled his capsule's attitude during the flight using a hand controller, though the arc itself was ballistic and unpowered.
events.revealBlurb: May 5, 1961 — Freedom 7. Shepard had been suited up and waiting in the capsule for four hours through repeated launch delays. At one point he radioed mission control: "Why don't you fix your little problem and light this candle?" His answer came 15 minutes later. He was weightless for only 5 minutes of the flight.

events.title: First Crewed Lunar Orbit
events.blurb: Three astronauts fired their Service Propulsion System engine on Christmas Eve to enter orbit 112 km above the Moon — the first humans to leave Earth's gravitational sphere of influence and orbit another world. During the mission's ninth orbit, Bill Anders photographed a crescent Earth rising over the lunar horizon, producing what became one of the most widely reproduced photographs in history.
events.revealBlurb: December 24, 1968 — Apollo 8. An estimated one billion people across 64 countries watched the Christmas Eve television broadcast in which the crew read the opening verses of Genesis. The Earthrise photograph is credited with catalyzing the environmental movement; the image appeared on the first Earth Day poster in 1970.

events.title: Voyager 1 Launch
events.blurb: NASA launched Voyager 1 on a trajectory exploiting a once-in-176-year alignment of the outer planets, allowing a single spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn using gravitational slingshots. The probe carries a gold-plated copper phonograph record containing sounds, music, and images representing life on Earth, selected by a committee chaired by Carl Sagan.
events.revealBlurb: September 5, 1977 — Voyager 1. It launched 16 days after its twin, Voyager 2, yet arrived at Jupiter first due to a faster trajectory. In 2012 it became the first human-made object to enter interstellar space. As of 2024 it is more than 24 billion km from Earth — so far that its radio signals, traveling at light speed, take over 22 hours to arrive.

events.title: Water Confirmed on the Moon
events.blurb: India's Chandrayaan-1 Moon Impact Probe detected spectral signatures consistent with water molecules during its 25-minute controlled descent to the lunar south pole, with readings from a mass spectrometer increasing steadily as the probe flew toward higher latitudes. Three instruments on the orbiting spacecraft corroborated the finding, confirming that water ice is present across the lunar surface.
events.revealBlurb: November 14, 2008 — Chandrayaan-1/MIP. The probe was decorated with the Indian national flag and crashed intentionally near Shackleton Crater at 85° south — making India the fourth nation to place an object on the Moon. The water discovery reversed decades of scientific consensus that the Moon was bone dry, reshaping plans for every future lunar base concept.

events.title: Brunelleschi's Dome Completed
events.blurb: A Florentine goldsmith turned architect completed, after 16 years of work without scaffolding, a vast octagonal dome over the crossing of a century-old cathedral. The double-shelled design, assembled with four million bricks in a self-supporting herringbone pattern, spanned 42 metres — wider than any dome built since Roman antiquity. The cathedral had stood domeless for over a century, waiting for someone to figure out how.
events.revealBlurb: August 25, 1436 — consecrated. Filippo Brunelleschi at Santa Maria del Fiore, Florence. He refused to leave blueprints, fearing competitors would steal the ideas. Part of the technique was rediscovered only in the 20th century through forensic study of the bricks.

events.title: Luther Posts the 95 Theses
events.blurb: A 33-year-old German university theologian sent his local archbishop a letter enclosing a 95-point list of academic propositions challenging the papal indulgence system — the practice of selling forgiveness of sins. By tradition, he also posted the Latin theses on the door of his university church, which served as a community bulletin board. Copies reached print within weeks and spread across Germany. He had intended academic debate; he ignited the Protestant Reformation.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1517 — Martin Luther at Wittenberg Castle Church. Most scholars doubt the physical nailing-to-the-door story; the letter to Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz is well-documented. October 31 is now celebrated as Reformation Day in many Protestant countries.

events.title: First Circumnavigation Complete
events.blurb: The last seaworthy ship of a Spanish expedition that had set out three years earlier with five vessels dropped anchor in the Guadalquivir River in Spain — the first ship ever to return to its port of departure after sailing completely around the world. Of the 270 men who had departed, 18 returned alive. Its captain, though no longer the expedition's original commander — who had been killed in the Philippines — had personally sailed the ship the entire way home.
events.revealBlurb: September 6, 1522 — Juan Sebastián Elcano aboard the Victoria. The voyage proved the earth was circumnavigable, and also forced the first adjustment of the ship's log by a day (a precursor to the concept of the International Date Line). Elcano himself died at sea in 1526, three ships into another expedition.

events.title: Elizabeth I Accession
events.blurb: A 25-year-old unmarried princess, the daughter of a beheaded second queen who had once been declared a bastard, became Queen of England on the death of her half-sister. She had survived imprisonment and political marginalization under her sister's Catholic restoration. Her 44-year reign would see the English settlement of Ireland, the defeat of the Spanish Armada, the flowering of Shakespeare, and the establishment of a Protestant national church still in existence.
events.revealBlurb: November 17, 1558 — Elizabeth I Tudor succeeds Mary I. She reportedly received the news sitting under an oak tree at Hatfield House. She never married, styled herself the "Virgin Queen," and died at 69. The state of Virginia — briefly colonized under her — is named for her.

events.title: Edict of Nantes
events.blurb: The first Bourbon king of France, a former Protestant who had converted to Catholicism to secure his crown ("Paris is worth a Mass"), issued an edict guaranteeing Protestant Huguenots freedom of worship in specific towns, civil equality, and the right to maintain their own fortified places. The compromise ended 36 years of Wars of Religion and was the most expansive grant of religious toleration any European state had yet made. His grandson would revoke it 87 years later.
events.revealBlurb: April 13, 1598 — Henry IV of France. Louis XIV revoked it in 1685, triggering a Protestant exodus of perhaps 400,000 skilled workers. Henry IV himself was assassinated by a Catholic fanatic in 1610.

events.title: Bombay Talkies Founded
events.blurb: A studio established in Malad, Bombay, by a London-trained filmmaker and his aristocratic actress-wife drew European technical talent — German cameramen, British equipment — to build India's first modern film facility with synchronised sound stages and a Western-style star system. It launched the careers of Dilip Kumar, Ashok Kumar, and Madhubala within its first fifteen years.
events.revealBlurb: April 15, 1934 — founded by Himanshu Rai and Devika Rani. Rai died in 1940 while the studio was mid-production; Devika Rani, then 32, took sole control and ran it for another nine years. The studio was where a young Dilip Kumar walked in looking for work and was handed a contract he barely understood.

events.title: Hum Aapke Hain Koun..! Released
events.blurb: A fourteen-song, over-three-hour family wedding drama that critics pre-screened and privately predicted was an unreleasable disaster became, on release, the first Hindi film to gross ₹1 billion — selling 74 million tickets domestically, the highest footfall for any Hindi film since the 1990s. The industry pivoted overnight toward family-oriented, non-violent spectacle.
events.revealBlurb: August 5, 1994 — director Sooraj Barjatya, a sequel of sorts to his earlier Maine Pyar Kiya. Salman Khan and Madhuri Dixit were cast against type as wholesome leads. The film ran in a Mumbai multiplex for over three years without leaving screens.

events.title: Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge Released
events.blurb: A romance about two Non-Resident Indians falling in love on a Eurorail trip before battling parental disapproval opened in Bombay that autumn and never fully left: it ran continuously at one Mumbai cinema for over two decades, setting a record no Indian film has matched. Its climactic train-platform scene became shorthand for every subsequent Bollywood love story.
events.revealBlurb: October 20, 1995 — Aditya Chopra's directorial debut, age 23. He refused to watch the film with an audience for years. Shah Rukh Khan initially had reservations about the role. The film ran at Mumbai's Maratha Mandir theatre without interruption until 2023 — 1,278 weeks.

events.title: "Naatu Naatu" Wins Academy Award
events.blurb: A Telugu period action film about two real freedom fighters reimagined as friends on opposite sides of a colonial conflict produced a seven-minute dance sequence that, when performed live at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles, brought an Oscars audience to its feet. The song became the first from an Indian film to win the Academy Award for Best Original Song.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 2023 — the 95th Academy Awards. Composer M.M. Keeravani and lyricist Chandrabose won. Director S.S. Rajamouli's RRR had not been submitted as India's official Oscar entry — it qualified independently through its US distributor. Singers Rahul Sipligunj and Kaala Bhairava performed barefoot on the Oscars stage.

events.title: Jawan Released
events.blurb: A Tamil director's Hindi-film debut — a dual-role action thriller mixing vigilante politics with hospital corruption — earned ₹75 crore on its opening day, making it the highest-opening-day gross in Hindi cinema at the time, then crossed ₹600 crore domestically, becoming the first Hindi film to do so. Its release capped a year in which its star reclaimed the top of the industry after a decade's absence.
events.revealBlurb: September 7, 2023 — directed by Atlee. Shah Rukh Khan's return, following Pathaan earlier that year, made 2023 the most commercially dominant single-year performance by any one actor in Bollywood history. The film's opening credits featured cameos by over thirty prominent South Indian actors.

events.title: September 11 Attacks
events.blurb: Nineteen hijackers affiliated with al-Qaeda commandeered four commercial airliners on a Tuesday morning, crashing two into the twin towers of a Manhattan financial complex, one into a Pentagon wing, and one into a Pennsylvania field after passengers fought back. Both World Trade Center towers collapsed within two hours. 2,977 people died. The attacks reshaped American foreign policy, launched two wars that lasted the next two decades, and redefined commercial aviation security for a generation.
events.revealBlurb: September 11, 2001 — orchestrated by Osama bin Laden. United States entered Afghanistan in October 2001 and Iraq in March 2003. The 9/11 Memorial & Museum opened on the site in 2014; One World Trade Center, topped out in 2013, is the tallest building in the Western Hemisphere.

events.title: Britney Shaves Her Head
events.blurb: A 25-year-old American pop star walked into a Los Angeles hair salon at 8 PM, asked a stylist to shave her head completely, and when the stylist refused, picked up the electric clippers and did it herself. Paparazzi captured the scene through the salon window. Images went global within hours, becoming an emblem of a period of intensely public personal struggle — divorce, custody battles, reportage, and tabloid harassment. She would be placed under conservatorship nine months later.
events.revealBlurb: February 16, 2007 — Britney Spears at Esther's Haircutting Studio, Tarzana, CA. The conservatorship lasted 13 years, ending in November 2021 after the #FreeBritney movement. Her 2023 memoir "The Woman in Me" describes the head-shaving as a reaction to feeling over-managed and pressured by the industry.

events.title: Kanye Interrupts Taylor Swift
events.blurb: A 32-year-old Chicago rapper walked onstage at a New York awards show as a 19-year-old country-pop singer was beginning her acceptance speech for Best Female Video, took the microphone from her, and declared that another nominee deserved to win. The interruption shocked the audience; the singer stood silently holding the award. It seeded a long-running and increasingly baroque public rivalry between the two performers that would include her several songs about him, his 2016 song about her, and a leaked phone call.
events.revealBlurb: September 13, 2009 — Kanye West interrupting Taylor Swift at the MTV VMAs. The other nominee Kanye was championing: Beyoncé. Beyoncé won the night's top award and gave her acceptance time back to Swift. The moment has replayed in the Swift-West feud for over 15 years.

events.title: Balloon Boy Hoax
events.blurb: A Colorado family reported that their 6-year-old son had been carried aloft in a homemade silver mylar weather balloon that had drifted off from their backyard. National news networks covered the balloon's two-hour, 80-kilometre flight live, interrupting regular programming. The balloon landed empty. The boy was found hiding in the family attic. Within a day, the father admitted the whole thing had been a publicity stunt, hoping to land the family a reality-TV show.
events.revealBlurb: October 15, 2009 — Heene family, Fort Collins, CO. The father Richard Heene was convicted of a felony and served 30 days; the mother Mayumi got misdemeanor charges. The Heenes reportedly received a pardon from Colorado governor Jared Polis in December 2020.

events.title: Lady Gaga's Meat Dress
events.blurb: A 24-year-old American pop singer arrived at a New York awards show wearing an outfit made from 50 pounds of raw Argentine beef — flank steak fashioned into a sleeveless dress, a matching hat, a handbag, and shoes. She told a late-night host the ensemble was a protest against a military policy excluding openly gay service members. PETA criticized it; steak prices nationwide did not apparently change. The dress was later preserved as beef jerky and displayed at the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame.
events.revealBlurb: September 12, 2010 — Lady Gaga (Stefani Germanotta) at the MTV VMAs. Designer Franc Fernandez. The dress won her five VMAs that night, including Video of the Year for "Bad Romance." It is now permanently on display in Cleveland.

events.title: Atari 2600 Launches
events.blurb: For the first time, a home console used interchangeable cartridges — meaning the same hardware could play a new game every week. Atari sold 250,000 units in the first months at $199 apiece. Within three years the living room had replaced the arcade as the primary venue for video games.
events.revealBlurb: September 11, 1977 — Atari released the Video Computer System (renamed 2600 in 1982). By 1982, 15 million 2600s had been sold and the console was generating $2 billion in annual revenue.

events.title: Super Mario Bros. Released in Japan
events.blurb: A moustachioed Italian plumber leaping over mushrooms and sliding down pipes became the defining character of interactive entertainment. The game shipped as a pack-in with the Nintendo Entertainment System and single-handedly revived an industry that had collapsed two years earlier under the weight of its own shovelware.
events.revealBlurb: September 13, 1985 — Super Mario Bros. launched for Nintendo's Famicom in Japan. It sold over 40 million copies, a record that stood until Wii Sports in 2009. Designer Shigeru Miyamoto built the entire world around the mechanic of a running jump.

events.title: Doom Uploaded to the Internet
events.blurb: At midnight, id Software attempted to upload its new game to a university FTP server. So many people were already waiting that the network collapsed. When the file finally went live, 10,000 simultaneous downloads crashed it again. Doom popularised the first-person shooter genre, the shareware distribution model, online multiplayer, user-generated mods, and the moral panic about video game violence — all within a few months.
events.revealBlurb: December 10, 1993 — id Software uploaded Doom to an FTP server at the University of Wisconsin–Madison after working 30 consecutive hours. The game sold over 2 million retail copies and was installed on an estimated 10 million PCs via shareware by 1995.

events.title: Final Fantasy VII Released in Japan
events.blurb: A Japanese role-playing game with pre-rendered 3D backgrounds, full orchestral-style music, and a story involving ecological collapse and corporate villainy sold out PlayStation consoles across Japan before it even launched. On release day it sold 1.75 million copies in a single country in a single day.
events.revealBlurb: January 31, 1997 — Final Fantasy VII launched in Japan for PlayStation. It sold 2.3 million copies in its first three days and over 6 million by 1998. Its western release September 7, 1997, introduced the JRPG genre to millions. The 2020 remake sold over 7 million copies in under four days.

events.title: Oculus Rift Kickstarter Campaign Launches
events.blurb: A 19-year-old in his parents' garage had spent years building virtual reality headsets from scavenged parts. His Kickstarter campaign asked for $250,000 to build a developer kit. It raised $2.4 million from nearly 10,000 backers. Two years later, Facebook acquired his company for $2 billion.
events.revealBlurb: August 1, 2012 — Palmer Luckey launched the Oculus Rift Kickstarter, raising 974% of its $250,000 goal. Facebook (now Meta) acquired Oculus VR in March 2014 for approximately $2 billion.

events.title: Integrated Circuit Demonstrated
events.blurb: An engineer at a Dallas electronics company demonstrated a germanium chip the size of a paperclip with a working oscillator etched directly onto its surface — the first integrated circuit, combining multiple transistors, resistors, and capacitors into a single monolithic piece of semiconductor. The invention would shrink electronic components by orders of magnitude every decade for the next half-century.
events.revealBlurb: September 12, 1958 — Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments. Robert Noyce at Fairchild developed a similar design independently a few months later using silicon; his is the variant the industry actually used. Kilby won the 2000 Nobel; Noyce had died in 1990 and so was ineligible.

events.title: Microsoft Founded
events.blurb: A 19-year-old Harvard sophomore and his 22-year-old friend, working out of a cheap room in an Albuquerque motel, formally established a partnership to develop software for microcomputers. Their first product had been a BASIC interpreter for the Altair 8800, licensed to the kit's manufacturer. The contract paid royalties per machine sold. Within seven years they would own the personal-computer operating system industry.
events.revealBlurb: April 4, 1975 — Bill Gates and Paul Allen. Originally "Micro-Soft." They moved to the Seattle suburb of Bellevue in 1979 and to Redmond in 1986. Allen left the company in 1983 after being diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma; he recovered, founded other businesses, died in 2018.

events.title: IBM PC Released
events.blurb: The world's dominant mainframe computer maker released a small desktop machine built, unusually for the company, from off-the-shelf parts — an Intel 8088 processor, an operating system licensed from Microsoft, components any competitor could buy. Business customers trusted the name and bought millions. The design's open specifications led to a decade of "IBM compatible" clones that collectively made the Intel/Microsoft duopoly inevitable.
events.revealBlurb: August 12, 1981 — IBM PC model 5150. It had 16KB of RAM and no hard drive. IBM's decision to source DOS from Microsoft, rather than write it in-house, is usually cited as the great strategic error of 20th-century computing. Gates retained all distribution rights.

events.title: Windows 95 Launch
events.blurb: A Seattle-area software company staged one of the biggest product launches in technology history — a billion-dollar worldwide marketing campaign including exclusive use of the Rolling Stones' "Start Me Up," late-night TV appearances, lighting up the Empire State Building, and midnight retail store openings with thousands queuing to buy the shrink-wrapped boxes. The product introduced the Start menu, taskbar, and long file names to mass audiences.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 1995 — Microsoft Windows 95. It sold 7 million copies in the first five weeks. Jay Leno hosted the launch event. The product was legitimately a leap forward over Windows 3.1 — and a reminder that one company now effectively controlled the world's desktop computers.

events.title: Google Founded
events.blurb: Two Stanford doctoral students incorporated a search engine company whose name derived from the mathematical term for 10 to the power of 100. Their PageRank algorithm ranked results by treating hyperlinks as votes, producing more relevant results than the keyword-frequency systems that dominated at the time.

events.title: Shays' Rebellion: Armed Farmers Storm Springfield Armory
events.blurb: A force of roughly 1,500 debt-ridden Massachusetts farmers led by Revolutionary War veteran Daniel Shays marched on the federal arsenal at Springfield in the depths of winter, hoping to seize weapons and overthrow a state government that was seizing their farms for unpaid taxes. State militia repelled the attack with cannon fire, killing four rebels — but the uprising terrified the nation's leaders into convening the Philadelphia Convention that produced the Constitution.
events.revealBlurb: January 25, 1787 — Springfield, Massachusetts. Daniel Shays was never caught and was eventually pardoned. George Washington, alarmed by news of the rebellion at his Mount Vernon retirement, came out of retirement to preside over the Constitutional Convention it helped cause.

events.title: Haymarket Bombing, Chicago
events.blurb: At a labor rally in Chicago's Haymarket Square called to protest the police killing of striking workers the previous day, an unknown person threw a dynamite bomb into a column of police officers, killing seven officers and at least four civilians in the ensuing explosion and gunfire. The incident became the defining trauma of American labor radicalism and led to the hanging of four men for conspiracy, despite the bomber's identity never being established.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1886 — Haymarket Square, Chicago. Nobody has ever been identified as the bomber. Governor John Altgeld pardoned the surviving defendants in 1893, calling the trial a miscarriage of justice — and was destroyed politically for it. The date May 4 became International Workers' Day in much of the world as a result of the Haymarket executions.

events.title: Cuban Missile Crisis: JFK Announces Naval Blockade
events.blurb: On the 22nd of that month, President John F. Kennedy delivered a nationally televised address revealing that U.S. reconnaissance aircraft had discovered Soviet nuclear missile installations under construction in Cuba — 90 miles from Florida — and announcing a naval "quarantine" to prevent further weapons deliveries. For 13 days, the United States and Soviet Union stood closer to nuclear war than at any other moment in history before or since.
events.revealBlurb: October 22, 1962 — Washington, D.C. Kennedy called it a "quarantine" because a blockade is an act of war under international law. Soviet ships turned around on October 24. The secret resolution involved the U.S. quietly removing its Jupiter missiles from Turkey — a concession Kennedy couldn't publicly acknowledge for decades.

events.title: September 11 Terrorist Attacks
events.blurb: That morning, 19 al-Qaeda hijackers commandeered four commercial aircraft and flew two into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center, one into the Pentagon, and a fourth — whose passengers revolted and forced the plane down — into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. The attacks killed 2,977 people and triggered the United States' longest wars, a sweeping reorganization of domestic security, and a generation of political consequence.
events.revealBlurb: September 11, 2001 — New York, Virginia, Pennsylvania. The North Tower stood 102 minutes after impact; the South Tower collapsed first, 56 minutes after being hit, because the plane struck lower floors. The 9/11 Commission found no credible evidence of state sponsorship by any foreign government.

events.title: Lehman Brothers Collapses: 2008 Financial Crisis
events.blurb: Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy — the largest bankruptcy in American history, with over $600 billion in assets — triggering a global financial panic that erased more than $10 trillion in U.S. household wealth and produced the worst economic downturn since the 1930s. The failure stemmed from the firm's enormous exposure to mortgage-backed securities tied to a collapsing housing market.
events.revealBlurb: September 15, 2008 — New York City. The Federal Reserve and Treasury had just rescued Bear Stearns and Fannie Mae but declined to backstop Lehman. The Dow dropped 504 points that day — and lost another 33% over the next three months. TARP, a $700 billion bank rescue program, was signed into law 19 days later.

events.title: Lascaux Cave Paintings
events.blurb: In a limestone complex in southwestern France, Paleolithic artists over multiple generations painted some 6,000 bulls, deer, horses, and abstract signs along narrow corridors and a soaring "Hall of the Bulls" as large as a Romanesque nave. The largest painted bull is over five metres long. The cave was rediscovered in 1940 by four teenagers and their dog investigating a tree that had been uprooted by a storm.
events.revealBlurb: c. 17,000 BCE — Montignac, Dordogne. The original cave was closed to visitors in 1963 when tourist breath and carbon dioxide began damaging the pigments. Lascaux II, III, and IV — increasingly faithful replicas — have been opened to the public.

events.title: Parthenon Marbles Completed
events.blurb: Under the direction of a single master sculptor, a team of Athenian craftsmen completed the exterior sculptural programme of a temple on a fortified limestone hill above their city — a continuous carved frieze 160 metres long depicting a civic religious procession, plus 92 metopes and two pediments. The sculptures were painted in vivid colours; the bleached white appearance known to modern viewers is an accident of weathering.
events.revealBlurb: c. 438 BCE — Phidias, chief sculptor of the Parthenon in Athens. Lord Elgin removed about half the surviving marbles between 1801 and 1812 and sold them to the British Museum. Greece has been asking for them back for over 200 years.

events.title: Michelangelo's David Unveiled
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Florentine sculptor unveiled a 5.17-metre marble nude of a biblical hero, carved over three years from a single block of Carrara marble that had been rejected by two earlier sculptors as flawed. The statue was intended for the rooftop of a cathedral; a committee that included Leonardo da Vinci decided the work was too significant to put out of sight and instead installed it in the main square of the city.
events.revealBlurb: September 8, 1504 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. Moving it from the workshop to the Piazza della Signoria took 40 men 4 days. The statue was damaged by a mob in 1527 and by a 1991 attack with a hammer; it now stands indoors at the Accademia, where a copy watches over the piazza.

events.title: Armory Show Opens
events.blurb: An exhibition at a New York National Guard armory introduced American audiences to European modernism at industrial scale — 1,300 paintings and sculptures by artists most had never heard of, including Matisse, Picasso, Duchamp, and Brancusi. Duchamp's "Nude Descending a Staircase No. 2" was ridiculed by a popular cartoonist as "explosion in a shingle factory" and drew crowds for exactly that reason. The show moved on to Chicago and Boston and is credited with changing the course of American art.
events.revealBlurb: February 17 to March 15, 1913 — the 69th Regiment Armory, Lexington Avenue, NYC. Around 90,000 people visited in New York alone. Theodore Roosevelt wrote a mostly-baffled review; a reproduction of the "Nude" was burned in effigy at the Chicago Art Institute.

events.title: Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans
events.blurb: A 33-year-old former commercial illustrator exhibited 32 canvases, each showing a single can of condensed soup — one for each of the 32 varieties the food company then sold. He had painted them by projecting photographic images onto the canvas and tracing. The show sold modestly: five of the canvases went for $100 each; the gallery owner bought them back and later resold the whole set for $2 million.
events.revealBlurb: July 9, 1962 — Ferus Gallery, Los Angeles, Andy Warhol. The artist said he ate Campbell's soup every day for 20 years. The set is now in MoMA. Warhol would soon apply the same silk-screen methods to Marilyn Monroe, Jackie Kennedy, and Elvis.

events.title: Lost Premieres
events.blurb: A serialized drama from ABC premiered its first episode — a 92-minute pilot for which the network had spent $14 million, then the most expensive pilot in TV history. A passenger jet crashes on a mysterious Pacific island; the survivors discover polar bears, giant submerged statues, smoke monsters, and hatches. The show pioneered the era of densely plotted serialized TV that viewers would parse online week by week, and ran for six increasingly contested seasons.
events.revealBlurb: September 22, 2004 — ABC, creators J.J. Abrams, Damon Lindelof, Jeffrey Lieber. Cast included Matthew Fox, Evangeline Lilly, Josh Holloway, and Jorge Garcia. The finale on May 23, 2010 drew 13.5 million viewers and a generation-defining debate over whether it had all made sense.

events.title: Oprah's "You Get a Car!"
events.blurb: An American daytime talk-show host opened her show's 19th-season premiere by giving a brand-new compact sedan to each of 276 audience members who, she said, had been nominated by loved ones as desperately needing a new vehicle. She turned to a different audience section and shouted: "You get a car! You get a car!" each audience member in turn. The sustained joy — and the full-volume shouting — became a lasting cultural moment captured in countless memes and parodies.
events.revealBlurb: September 13, 2004 — Oprah Winfrey on The Oprah Winfrey Show. The cars were Pontiac G6 sedans donated by General Motors, which covered the ~$7 million cost as a promotion. Audience members were reportedly shocked to discover the IRS expected them to pay tax on the "gift" of around $7,000.

events.title: Michael Jackson Dies
events.blurb: A 50-year-old American singer widely regarded as the most successful pop star of his generation died of cardiac arrest at his rented Los Angeles home while preparing for a 50-concert comeback tour in London. His personal physician was later convicted of involuntary manslaughter for administering propofol, a surgical anesthetic, to help him sleep. His death prompted an outpouring of grief that crashed major websites and sold over 35 million of his records in the following six months.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 2009 — Michael Jackson. His physician, Conrad Murray, was sentenced to 4 years and served 2. His public memorial on July 7 drew 31 million U.S. TV viewers. The "This Is It" concert film, compiled from rehearsal footage, grossed $261 million posthumously.

events.title: William and Kate Wedding
events.blurb: The 28-year-old second-in-line heir to the British throne married his 29-year-old university sweetheart at Westminster Abbey in London before a congregation of 1,900 and a global TV audience estimated at 2 billion. The bride wore a long-sleeved ivory lace gown; the couple kissed twice on the Buckingham Palace balcony. The marriage, closely followed by the British tabloids for years, has so far produced three children and remained notably less turbulent than the equivalent royal marriage of the generation before.
events.revealBlurb: April 29, 2011 — Prince William and Catherine Middleton. William succeeded his father Charles as Prince of Wales when Charles became king in September 2022. Their three children, in line to the throne: George (2013), Charlotte (2015), Louis (2018).

events.title: "The Dress" Goes Viral
events.blurb: A 21-year-old Scottish woman posted a photograph of a dress on her Tumblr account asking for help settling a family argument — was it black and blue, or white and gold? The photo went viral overnight. Approximately 40 percent of viewers saw it as white and gold; 50 percent as black and blue. Vision scientists spent months examining why. The actual dress, in real life, was black and blue. The phenomenon became a landmark case study in how individual visual perception varies based on assumptions about ambient lighting.
events.revealBlurb: February 26, 2015 — Cecilia Bleasdale's photograph, posted by Caitlin McNeill. Roman Originals, who made the dress, saw a 560 percent spike in sales. Neuroscientists published papers on it for years. It revived serious research into color constancy and top-down visual processing.

events.title: Virgil's Aeneid
events.blurb: A 51-year-old Roman poet died with his commissioned national epic not quite finished, asking on his deathbed that the unfinished manuscript be burned. The emperor he had spent a decade writing it for overruled him. The twelve-book poem traced the mythical origins of Rome to a Trojan prince fleeing the burning city. It became, and remains, the canonical literary masterpiece of Latin civilization.
events.revealBlurb: 19 BCE — Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro). Emperor Augustus saved the text. Virgil's funeral procession was attended by the emperor himself. Dante took Virgil as his guide through Hell and Purgatory in The Divine Comedy; Milton modeled Paradise Lost on the Aeneid.

events.title: Dante Completes Divine Comedy
events.blurb: A 56-year-old exiled Florentine poet completed the third and final part of a long allegorical poem describing his journey through Hell, Purgatory, and Heaven, guided by a Roman poet and his earthly beloved. Written in Italian rather than Latin, it pulled the vernacular into literary respectability. He died within months of finishing.
events.revealBlurb: 1320 — Dante Alighieri. He had been exiled from Florence in 1302 over factional politics; he never returned. The last 13 cantos of Paradiso were missing for months after his death until his son Jacopo found them in a secret cavity in a wall, supposedly after Dante appeared in a dream.

events.title: Chaucer's Canterbury Tales
events.blurb: An English civil servant in his mid-fifties died leaving unfinished a collection of stories told by pilgrims riding from Southwark to a Kentish cathedral shrine. Written in Middle English rather than French or Latin, the work demonstrated the poetic range of the English vernacular across a social spectrum — knights, millers, cooks, pardoners, the famously bawdy Wife of Bath. Only 24 of a planned 120 tales were ever completed.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1400 — Geoffrey Chaucer. He is often called the father of English literature. Roughly 80 manuscripts survive; the earliest complete ones date from the 1410s. The Wife of Bath's Tale became an early feminist touchstone.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Printed
events.blurb: A goldsmith in a Rhine-valley city completed the first book printed in Europe using movable metal type — a Latin Bible set in 42 lines per page, bound in 180 copies. His press combined existing technologies — oil-based ink, a wine-press frame, cast-metal punches — into an invention that would be blamed for everything from the Reformation to the Renaissance to modern literacy.
events.revealBlurb: 1455 — Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz. Forty-nine copies are known to survive; roughly twenty are complete. Gutenberg himself was sued by his financier the same year and lost the press.

events.title: Leaves of Grass Published
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Brooklyn printer, essayist, and newspaper editor self-published a small quarto of 12 unrhymed, unmetered poems celebrating the American body politic in a language saturated with sexual frankness. It drew praise from Ralph Waldo Emerson and denunciation from almost everyone else. The author kept expanding and revising the volume for the rest of his life; the final 1892 "deathbed edition" contained over 400 poems.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1855 — Walt Whitman, self-published because no publisher would take it. He set much of it himself at a Brooklyn print shop. His job at the Department of the Interior was terminated in 1865 after the Secretary read a copy and called it obscene.

events.title: Elizabeth Blackwell Graduates
events.blurb: A 28-year-old English-born schoolteacher, who had been admitted to a small upstate New York medical college as a joke when the all-male student body voted unanimously to accept her application, graduated first in her class to become the first woman in the United States to earn a medical degree. She had been refused admission by 20 other schools. Her younger sister would become the third.
events.revealBlurb: January 23, 1849 — Geneva Medical College, Geneva, NY. No American hospital would employ her; she moved to Paris and London for clinical training. She later founded a medical college for women and practiced for decades, treating patients the profession otherwise ignored.

events.title: New Zealand Grants Women's Suffrage
events.blurb: The governor of a British colony in the South Pacific gave royal assent to an electoral act adding "and women" to the existing definition of qualified voters, making the colony the first self-governing country in the world to grant women the national franchise. Roughly 90,000 women registered within weeks; 82 percent of them turned out for the first subsequent election.
events.revealBlurb: September 19, 1893 — campaigners including Kate Sheppard delivered a petition a quarter of a kilometre long with nearly 32,000 signatures. The date is now Suffrage Day in New Zealand. Sheppard appears on the country's ten-dollar note.

events.title: Roe v. Wade
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that the right to privacy implicit in the 14th Amendment protected a woman's decision to terminate a pregnancy, striking down most state abortion laws. The ruling established a three-trimester framework balancing state interests against individual rights. It would remain the governing precedent for 49 years, until its overturn in 2022 returned abortion regulation to the states.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1973 — plaintiff "Jane Roe" was Norma McCorvey, who never actually had the abortion. She changed her position on the issue multiple times before her death in 2017. The ruling was overturned by Dobbs v. Jackson on June 24, 2022.

events.title: Battle of the Sexes
events.blurb: A 29-year-old women's tennis champion beat a 55-year-old former men's Wimbledon champion in straight sets at a televised exhibition match at a Houston indoor arena, before 30,000 spectators and an estimated 90 million television viewers worldwide. The older player had spent months mocking women's tennis in the press; he entered the arena on a rickshaw pulled by models in skimpy outfits and gave her a Sugar Daddy lollipop at the net.
events.revealBlurb: September 20, 1973 — Billie Jean King beat Bobby Riggs 6-4, 6-3, 6-3 at the Houston Astrodome. King had threatened to boycott the US Open unless prize money was equal; Forest Hills agreed in time for the tournament that August — the first Slam to do so.

events.title: Ruth Bader Ginsburg Confirmed
events.blurb: A 60-year-old federal appeals court judge, a former ACLU lawyer who had successfully argued six of the era's most important gender-discrimination cases before the court she was now joining, was confirmed 96-3 as the second woman to sit on the U.S. Supreme Court. She would serve 27 years, becoming — somewhat unexpectedly for a cautious litigator — a late-life pop-culture icon on the Court's liberal wing.
events.revealBlurb: August 10, 1993 — nominated by Bill Clinton. She acquired the nickname "Notorious RBG" from a law student's Tumblr in 2013. She died September 18, 2020, enabling the confirmation of Amy Coney Barrett eight days before the presidential election.

events.title: Battles of Lexington and Concord
events.blurb: That spring morning, British regulars marching to seize a colonial weapons cache at Concord, Massachusetts, exchanged fire with local militia at Lexington before the colonists scattered; at Concord's North Bridge, a second volley triggered a running battle that chased the redcoats back to Boston. The day produced roughly 300 total casualties and the phrase "the shot heard round the world."
events.revealBlurb: April 19, 1775 — Lexington and Concord, Massachusetts. Nobody knows who fired first at Lexington — colonial accounts and British accounts flatly contradict each other. The phrase "shot heard round the world" was written by Ralph Waldo Emerson in 1837, over 60 years after the fact.

events.title: U.S. Constitution Signed
events.blurb: Fifty-five delegates meeting for four months in a Philadelphia state house, working in secret through a sweltering summer with the windows closed against spies, produced a seven-article document replacing the loose Articles of Confederation with a stronger federal framework. Thirty-nine of them signed. An 81-year-old Benjamin Franklin, who had been at nearly every session, pointed at the sun carved into George Washington's chair and said he was finally sure it was rising, not setting.
events.revealBlurb: September 17, 1787 — Independence Hall, Philadelphia. Ratified June 21, 1788 after New Hampshire became the ninth state to approve. The Constitution has been amended 27 times in 235 years — less than once per decade. A different Philadelphia-era document, the Bill of Rights, followed in 1791.

events.title: Louis XVI Executed
events.blurb: A former French king, convicted by the National Convention of treason for allegedly conspiring with foreign powers against the revolution, was beheaded by a relatively new device on a Paris square as drums drowned out the opening lines of the speech he attempted to deliver from the scaffold. His wife, an Austrian-born former queen, would meet the same end nine months later. The regicide radicalized the revolution's enemies and internal fears alike.
events.revealBlurb: January 21, 1793 — Louis XVI at the Place de la Révolution (now Place de la Concorde). The National Convention had voted 361-360 for death, a margin of one. His final words were cut off by drums: "People, I die innocent..." Marie Antoinette was executed October 16, 1793.

events.title: Coup of 18 Brumaire
events.blurb: A 30-year-old French artillery general, recently returned from an unsuccessful campaign in Egypt, led a coup against the five-man executive Directory that had ruled France for four years. He had political allies in the councils and military support on the ground; within two days the Directory was gone and a new three-consul system was in place with him as its dominant first consul. In name, the revolution continued. In effect, one-man rule had returned.
events.revealBlurb: November 9-10, 1799 — Napoleon Bonaparte at the Château de Saint-Cloud. He would crown himself emperor five years later. The Gregorian-calendar date in the French revolutionary calendar was 18-19 Brumaire, Year VIII.

events.title: Grito de Dolores
events.blurb: A 57-year-old Catholic priest in a rural Mexican town, learning that a conspiracy of criollo-elite revolutionaries had been uncovered, rang his church bell in the middle of the night to summon his parishioners and call for the overthrow of Spanish colonial rule. He led his ragged army of peasants and mestizos toward the capital; the colonial government crushed them within four months and he was shot. The rebellion he had started, though, continued for 11 more years.
events.revealBlurb: September 16, 1810 — Father Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla at Dolores, Guanajuato. The exact wording of his "grito" is not recorded. Hidalgo was captured in March 1811 and executed by firing squad on July 30, 1811. September 16 is Mexico's Independence Day; the President still rings the bell each year.

events.title: Asteroids Released by Atari
events.blurb: Drawing lines on a vector monitor to simulate drifting through space debris sounds modest. The game that resulted became Atari's best-selling arcade cabinet of all time, pulling in an estimated 10 million quarters per day at its peak. Demand was so extreme that Atari temporarily halted production of other games and shipped Asteroids units inside Lunar Lander cabinets just to get them out the door faster.
events.revealBlurb: November 1979 — Atari released Asteroids in North American arcades. It sold over 70,000 cabinets. The game's high score table was the first widely adopted public performance metric in gaming — and the first subject of documented high-score fraud.

events.title: Pac-Man Debuts in Japanese Arcades
events.blurb: A yellow circle eating dots and fleeing ghosts through a maze seemed like a peculiar bet in an era dominated by shoot-'em-ups. It became the highest-grossing arcade game ever made, the first video game character to achieve mass-market celebrity, and the template for an entirely new genre. Its creator wanted a game that women would actually want to play.
events.revealBlurb: May 22, 1980 — Namco's Puck-Man (renamed Pac-Man for Western markets to prevent vandalism) went on location test in Shibuya, Tokyo. By 1982 an estimated 30 billion quarters had been inserted into Pac-Man machines worldwide.

events.title: Nintendo Game Boy Launches in North America
events.blurb: Competing handhelds boasted colour screens and better hardware. Nintendo shipped a grey brick with a pea-green LCD and bundled it with a Soviet puzzle game about falling tetrominoes. The grey brick won. Within weeks every unit in the United States had sold out.
events.revealBlurb: July 31, 1989 — The Game Boy launched in North America at $89.99, selling 40,000 units on day one. The Game Boy line eventually sold 118 million units. The Japan launch had been April 21, 1989.

events.title: The Sims Released
events.blurb: A game in which you build a house and manage the life of a simulated person — feeding them, making them use the bathroom, watching them catch fire if left unattended too long — became the best-selling PC game of the year, and then 2001, and then the best-selling PC game of all time. More than half its players were women, permanently disproving every assumption the games industry held about its audience.
events.revealBlurb: February 4, 2000 — Maxis and EA released The Sims for Windows. It sold 1.77 million copies in North America in its first year. The Sims overtook Myst to become the best-selling PC game ever in 2002. The franchise has sold over 70 million copies.

events.title: Grand Theft Auto V Released
events.blurb: A crime game set in a fictionalised Los Angeles earned $800 million on its first day and $1 billion within three days — the fastest any entertainment product in history had reached that figure at that time. Guinness certified six world records on launch day. More than a decade later it continues to generate revenue through its online component.
events.revealBlurb: September 17, 2013 — GTA V launched for PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360. It broke six Guinness World Records including fastest entertainment property to gross $1 billion. The game has sold over 200 million copies. GTA Online continues to generate over $1 billion annually.

events.title: Hanging Gardens of Babylon
events.blurb: Tradition holds that a Babylonian king built a tiered rooftop garden at his palace for his wife, homesick for the mountainous landscape of her native Media. The structure — described by Greek writers as having stone terraces planted with trees and shrubs irrigated by an elaborate water-lifting machine — was counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. No archaeological evidence of them has ever been identified at Babylon, leading some scholars to believe they existed instead at Nineveh under a different king.
events.revealBlurb: c. 600 BCE — traditionally attributed to Nebuchadnezzar II. A leading alternative theory attributes them to Sennacherib at Nineveh, a century earlier. Of the Seven Wonders, only the Pyramids survive and the Hanging Gardens are the one whose very existence is still in question.

events.title: Great Wall of China Begun
events.blurb: The first emperor of a unified Chinese state, having conquered the six rival warring kingdoms, ordered existing regional defensive walls in the north linked into a continuous frontier fortification against nomadic incursions. A conscripted army of 300,000 labourers worked for years; many died on the project and were, according to tradition, buried in its foundations. The Ming-dynasty wall, which is what most modern visitors see, was rebuilt over a millennium later.
events.revealBlurb: c. 220 BCE — Qin Shi Huang. The visible stone-and-brick wall is largely Ming-dynasty (1368-1644), built with much better materials. The Qin wall was mostly earthen and only fragments survive. Total length, across all versions, has been measured at 21,196 km.

events.title: Leaning Tower of Pisa Begun
events.blurb: Construction began on a free-standing bell tower for the cathedral complex of an Italian city-state on the Tuscan coast. By the time three of its eight stories were finished five years later, the soft alluvial ground beneath the south side was already sinking noticeably. Construction was halted for nearly a century. When work resumed, builders attempted to compensate by building upper floors taller on the low side — so the tower is actually curved. It was completed 199 years after ground-breaking.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1173 — Pisa Cathedral bell tower. The tilt is currently about 3.97 degrees after stabilization work completed in 2008. Galileo is said to have dropped balls of different weights from it to demonstrate they fall at the same rate — the story is almost certainly apocryphal.

events.title: US Capitol Cornerstone Laid
events.blurb: The president of the newly independent United States — wearing a Masonic apron — laid the cornerstone of a new federal capitol building on a wooded hill above the banks of the Potomac River. The building was meant to house the U.S. Congress. The winning design, by a Scottish-trained amateur architect, was a neoclassical rotunda crowned with a low dome; later architects would replace the dome with a much taller cast-iron one during the Civil War.
events.revealBlurb: September 18, 1793 — George Washington at Jenkins Hill (now Capitol Hill), Washington, D.C. Designer: William Thornton. The current wedding-cake dome was built 1855-1866 by Thomas U. Walter and crowned with the Statue of Freedom during the Civil War. Slave labour built much of the original building.

events.title: Chrysler Building Completed
events.blurb: A 319-metre Manhattan skyscraper, topped with a radiator-cap-inspired sunburst spire, opened at the corner of 42nd Street and Lexington Avenue as the tallest building in the world. Its automotive-magnate patron had kept the spire a construction secret; it was assembled inside the tower's upper levels and then hoisted into place in 90 minutes, triumphing over a rival bank project down Wall Street that had briefly claimed the height title. The Empire State Building eclipsed it 11 months later.
events.revealBlurb: May 27, 1930 — architect William Van Alen for Walter Chrysler. The Art Deco ornamentation includes eagle gargoyles at the 61st floor and a 1,700-square-metre ceiling mural in the lobby. Van Alen was never paid his fee — Chrysler accused him of taking bribes from suppliers.

events.title: Little Rock Nine
events.blurb: Nine Black teenagers, escorted by federal troops, walked through the front doors of an Arkansas capital's previously all-white high school, three weeks after the governor had called out the National Guard to bar them. The images of the 101st Airborne at the schoolhouse door — bayonets fixed — broadcast on the nightly news forced a hostile public to confront massive resistance.
events.revealBlurb: September 25, 1957 — Central High School, Little Rock. President Eisenhower federalized the entire Arkansas National Guard to override Governor Orval Faubus. One of the nine, Elizabeth Eckford, was famously photographed walking alone through a screaming mob on an earlier attempt.

events.title: SNCC Founded
events.blurb: At a North Carolina conference convened by a veteran activist, 200 student sit-in leaders from across the South formed a new grassroots organization to coordinate direct-action campaigns independently of older civil rights groups. The students were younger, more confrontational, and willing to risk their lives; many became the foot soldiers of the Freedom Rides, Freedom Summer, and Selma.
events.revealBlurb: April 17, 1960 — Raleigh, NC. Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, commonly pronounced "snick." Organizer Ella Baker convinced the students to stay independent rather than fold into Martin Luther King's Southern Christian Leadership Conference. Stokely Carmichael led it during the "Black Power" turn in 1966.

events.title: Freedom Riders Depart
events.blurb: Thirteen volunteers — seven Black, six white — boarded buses in Washington, D.C. bound for New Orleans to test a recent Supreme Court ruling outlawing segregated interstate travel facilities. In Alabama their bus was firebombed outside Anniston and the riders beaten bloody by a mob in Birmingham. They kept riding. Subsequent waves continued through the summer.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1961 — sponsored by CORE. A 21-year-old John Lewis was among them and had his skull fractured. Attorney General Robert Kennedy called for a "cooling-off period;" CORE leader James Farmer replied: "We've been cooling off for 100 years."

events.title: 16th Street Baptist Church Bombing
events.blurb: A dynamite bomb planted by Klansmen exploded under the stone steps of a Black church in a Southern city on a Sunday morning, minutes before the 11:00 service. Four girls preparing for choir in the basement were killed; 22 others were injured. The bombing, eighteen days after the March on Washington, hardened national public opinion and accelerated passage of civil rights legislation.
events.revealBlurb: September 15, 1963 — Birmingham, Alabama. Victims: Addie Mae Collins, 14; Carol Denise McNair, 11; Carole Robertson, 14; Cynthia Wesley, 14. The four Klansmen responsible were slowly prosecuted over four decades; the last conviction came in 2002.

events.title: Martin Luther King Jr. Assassinated
events.blurb: Stepping onto the balcony outside Room 306 of a Tennessee motel where he was staying while supporting a sanitation workers' strike, the country's most prominent civil rights leader was shot once with a high-powered rifle from across the street. He died an hour later at a nearby hospital. He was 39. Riots broke out in more than 100 American cities within hours of the news.
events.revealBlurb: April 4, 1968 — Lorraine Motel, Memphis. His killer, escaped convict James Earl Ray, was captured in London two months later. The night before, King had ended a speech with: "I've been to the mountaintop. I may not get there with you, but we, as a people, will get to the Promised Land."

events.title: Columbus Makes Landfall
events.blurb: A Genoese navigator commanding three vessels landed on an island in the present-day Bahamas after 70 days at sea, believing he had reached islands off the coast of Asia. He planted a royal standard, claimed the land in the name of the Spanish Crown, and named the island San Salvador — its indigenous inhabitants called it Guanahani.

events.title: Cabral Reaches Brazil
events.blurb: A 33-year-old Portuguese nobleman commanding a 13-ship expedition bound for India — following Vasco da Gama's recent route — sailed so far west to catch favourable trade winds that he accidentally made landfall on a South American coast later named after a dyewood tree. He claimed it for Portugal under the six-year-old Tordesillas line and continued on to India. The accidental detour is the conventional starting point of Brazilian history.
events.revealBlurb: April 22, 1500 — Pedro Álvares Cabral in modern Bahia. He called the land "Ilha de Vera Cruz." Some historians think the "accidental" landfall was deliberate, responding to intelligence Portuguese mariners had gathered earlier. He lost six ships and over 100 men to storms en route onward to India.

events.title: Magellan's Fleet Departs
events.blurb: Five ships and 270 sailors departed from Sanlúcar de Barrameda under a Portuguese navigator flying a Spanish flag, carrying provisions for two years. Three years later, one battered ship and 18 survivors returned — the first vessels to circumnavigate the globe, though their commander had been killed in a Filipino skirmish partway through.

events.title: Magellan Sets Sail
events.blurb: A 39-year-old Portuguese-born captain, working for the Spanish crown because his own king had rejected his project, left a Sevillian port with five small ships and 270 men on a westward voyage to the spice-rich islands of Southeast Asia. He was convinced a sea passage through the Americas existed. He would find it — and a strait at the continent's southern tip is now named after him — but he would never see its other end.
events.revealBlurb: September 20, 1519 — Ferdinand Magellan. He was killed on the Philippine island of Mactan on April 27, 1521 by troops of the local chief Lapu-Lapu. One of his five ships completed the first circumnavigation — returning with 18 survivors and a load of cloves that covered the entire expedition's costs.

events.title: Cortés Reaches Tenochtitlán
events.blurb: A 34-year-old Spanish conquistador, in defiance of orders from the governor of Cuba who had tried to recall him, entered the causeway-linked lakeside capital of the Aztec Triple Alliance — a city of perhaps 200,000 people, one of the largest in the world, built on an island in a high-altitude lake. The Aztec emperor met him with courtesy, gifts, and quiet suspicion. Within two years the emperor would be dead and the city in ruins.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1519 — Hernán Cortés meets Moctezuma II in Tenochtitlán (modern Mexico City). The Spanish force was about 500 strong, augmented by thousands of Tlaxcalan allies who hated the Aztecs. Cortés had burned his own ships on the coast to prevent desertion.

events.title: Book of Optics Written
events.blurb: While under house arrest in Cairo, a scholar wrote a seven-volume treatise on optics that correctly explained vision as the eye receiving light reflected from objects — overturning the ancient Greek idea that the eye emits visual rays outward. The work described the camera obscura, the physics of refraction and reflection, and the psychology of perception, and became foundational for later optical science.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1021 CE — Ibn al-Haytham was reportedly placed under house arrest after failing to deliver an ambitious Nile-regulation project he had proposed to the Caliph. He feigned madness to avoid execution, and used the period of confinement productively. The Book of Optics was translated into Latin around 1200 CE and was cited extensively by Kepler, Descartes, and Galileo.

events.title: Animal Electricity Discovered
events.blurb: An Italian physician published a decade of experiments showing that the muscles of dead frogs could be made to contract when touched with two different metals — or when connected to a charged conductor — demonstrating that animal tissues themselves generate and respond to electrical currents. The finding launched the science of electrophysiology and inspired fierce debate about the nature of electricity and life.
events.revealBlurb: 1791 — Luigi Galvani called the phenomenon "animal electricity"; Alessandro Volta argued it was purely metallic electricity and invented the first battery to prove the point. Both were partly right. The argument inspired Mary Shelley: she attended a lecture on Galvanic reanimation and later wrote Frankenstein.

events.title: Special Relativity Paper Published
events.blurb: A 30-page paper demolished the concept of absolute time, arguing that the speed of light is the same for all observers regardless of their motion, and that simultaneity, length, and mass all depend on relative velocity. The paper contained no citations, because its author — a patent clerk working in his spare time — had arrived at the theory by pure thought experiment.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 1905 — one of four papers the same author submitted to Annalen der Physik that year, including one on Brownian motion and one that would later win the Nobel Prize for the photoelectric effect. The mass-energy equivalence paper (E=mc²) followed two months later.

events.title: Penicillin Discovered
events.blurb: Returning from vacation, a bacteriologist noticed a petri dish of Staphylococcus bacteria had been contaminated by a mold that had dissolved the surrounding bacterial colonies into clear halos. He cultured the mold — Penicillium notatum — and determined it produced a substance lethal to bacteria, naming it penicillin.

events.title: Neutron Discovered
events.blurb: A British physicist bombarded beryllium with alpha particles and detected a neutral radiation that could knock protons out of paraffin wax with remarkable force. Reasoning that gamma rays lacked the energy for such collisions, he concluded the radiation must consist of uncharged particles with roughly the mass of a proton — completing the basic structure of the atomic nucleus.
events.revealBlurb: February 27, 1932 — James Chadwick completed the decisive experiments in under two weeks. He mailed a letter to Nature titled "Possible Existence of a Neutron." Frédéric and Irène Joliot-Curie had the same data a month earlier but misidentified what they had found. Chadwick won the Nobel Prize in 1935.

events.title: Rubik's Cube Global Craze
events.blurb: A 3×3 mechanical puzzle cube invented six years earlier by a Hungarian architecture professor became a global bestseller after licensed international distribution began. Over 100 million units sold in the first three years. Books of solutions appeared on bestseller lists. The puzzle's simplicity — six colours, 43 quintillion possible states, a single solved configuration — caught people who had never bought a toy in their lives. World championships began in 1982.
events.revealBlurb: 1981 — Ernő Rubik had patented the cube in 1975; it went international in 1980. The first world championship was in Budapest, June 5, 1982; the current world record for solving it is under 3.05 seconds (Max Park, June 2023). The cube remains in continuous production.

events.title: Tylenol Murders
events.blurb: Seven people in the Chicago area died after taking over-the-counter acetaminophen capsules that had been laced with potassium cyanide by an unknown tamperer.
