The crisis triggered a nationwide recall of 31 million bottles, launched the tamper-resistant packaging industry, and reshaped pharmaceutical manufacturing standards permanently. Johnson & Johnson's swift and transparent response became a classic case study in crisis management. The killer was never identified.
events.revealBlurb: September 29-October 1, 1982 — seven deaths in Chicago suburbs. Pills had been purchased, tampered with, and returned to drugstore shelves. James William Lewis, a former suspect, died in 2023 maintaining his innocence. Tamper-proof packaging became a federal mandate within six months.

events.title: The Breakfast Club Released
events.blurb: A film about five high-school students from different cliques stuck together for a Saturday detention in the school library opened in American theatres. The cast — a nerd, a jock, a princess, a rebel, a weirdo — talked, argued, and bonded over 97 minutes in a script tight enough that one actor later claimed much of it felt improvised. The film defined a style of introspective teen comedy-drama the decade would become known for. It grossed $45 million on a $1 million budget.
events.revealBlurb: February 15, 1985 — John Hughes directing Emilio Estevez, Molly Ringwald, Judd Nelson, Ally Sheedy, and Anthony Michael Hall. Hughes had written the script in a single weekend, 1982. The final fist-pump shot, set to Simple Minds' "Don't You (Forget About Me)," became iconic.

events.title: Nevermind Released
events.blurb: A three-piece rock band from Aberdeen, Washington released their second album featuring a swimming infant reaching for a dollar bill on a fishhook. Within three months it had displaced a reigning pop star's record from the top of the Billboard 200, and its lead single's music video received more plays on music television than any previous video.

events.title: Friends Premieres
events.blurb: A half-hour NBC sitcom about six young adults — a food chef, an aspiring actor, a paleontologist, a masseuse, a restaurant hostess, and a data processor — sharing two Greenwich Village apartments premiered to middling reviews and moderate ratings. The show would run ten years, cement the demographic of "twentysomething in Manhattan" as a comedy staple, and command an unprecedented $1 million per episode per cast member in its final season. Its title sequence featured six friends splashing in a fountain.
events.revealBlurb: September 22, 1994 — Jennifer Aniston, Courteney Cox, Lisa Kudrow, Matt LeBlanc, Matthew Perry, David Schwimmer. Created by Marta Kauffman and David Crane. The cast negotiated as a union, a strategy that pushed their salary to the stratosphere. Perry died in 2023 at 54.

events.title: Battle of Salamis
events.blurb: A Greek allied fleet of roughly 370 triremes, lured into position by a false message from the Athenian commander, engaged a Persian fleet of perhaps 800 in the narrow straits between a small island and the Athenian mainland coast. The Persian ships, crowded in the strait, could not maneuver; the Greek triremes rammed them methodically for twelve hours. Over 200 Persian ships were sunk or captured. The Persian king watched the disaster unfold from a throne on the adjacent mainland.
events.revealBlurb: September 480 BCE — Themistocles, Athenian strategos. The Persian king was Xerxes I; he retreated to Asia with much of his army, leaving a smaller force that was destroyed at Plataea the following year. Aeschylus, who had fought at Salamis himself, wrote a play about it eight years later.

events.title: Alexander the Great Dies
events.blurb: A 32-year-old conqueror, having created an empire stretching from Macedonia to northwestern India in ten years of campaigning, died of fever (or poisoning — sources disagree) in a palace in a Mesopotamian capital while planning the next campaign, this one against Arabia. He left no clear heir; his generals divided the empire into warring successor states — the Hellenistic kingdoms — that shaped Mediterranean culture for the next three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: June 10 or 11, 323 BCE — Alexander III in Babylon. Asked on his deathbed to whom his empire should go, he reportedly said: "To the strongest." Competing theories for his death: malaria, typhoid, alcoholism, West Nile virus, poisoning by his general Antipater. His body was hijacked en route home by Ptolemy to Alexandria.

events.title: Battle of Cannae
events.blurb: Hannibal's army of roughly 50,000 men destroyed a Roman force of 80,000 in a single afternoon by letting the Roman center push forward into a concave line, then closing cavalry on both flanks until the entire legionary mass was encircled and butchered. Between 55,000 and 70,000 Romans died; senators threw handfuls of gold rings stripped from dead equestrians into a bowl to show Carthage the scale of the slaughter.
events.revealBlurb: August 2, 216 BCE, Apulia. The double-envelopment Hannibal used at Cannae became the template studied at military academies for 2,000 years. Hannibal's war elephants, his most famous asset, had all died before this battle.

events.title: Silk Road Opens
events.blurb: A Chinese imperial envoy returning from a long mission into Central Asia reported the existence of advanced civilizations to the west. His court began dispatching trade missions through the oasis routes of Central Asia; within a century, Chinese silk was appearing in Roman markets, and Mediterranean glass was showing up in Han-dynasty tombs. The overland trade network — not a single road but a braided complex — would carry goods, people, religions, and epidemics across Eurasia for 1,500 years.
events.revealBlurb: c. 130 BCE — Zhang Qian's second mission, under Emperor Wu of Han. The term "Silk Road" was coined by 19th-century German geographer Ferdinand von Richthofen; no one in antiquity used the phrase. Buddhism reached China along it; the Black Death would as well.

events.title: The Antonine Plague
events.blurb: Soldiers returning from campaigns in Parthia brought a disease — almost certainly smallpox — that spread from the eastern frontier through every province of the empire over fifteen years. The physician Galen, the most famous doctor of his age, documented symptoms in detail from Rome itself; at the plague's peak witnesses recorded 2,000 deaths per day in the capital alone.
events.revealBlurb: 165–180 CE. Galen's treatment recommendation included keeping patients warm and feeding them milk — the best care available, and completely ineffective. The plague killed co-emperor Lucius Verus in 169 CE and may have killed up to 10% of the empire's total population.

events.title: Monteverdi's Orfeo Premieres
events.blurb: A 39-year-old Italian composer staged a setting of the Orpheus myth at a ducal palace in a northern Italian city, combining recitative, arias, choruses, and instrumental ritornellos in a way earlier experimental works had only gestured at. The resulting five-act piece is considered the first opera that remains in the regular performance repertoire. Only two printed scores of the work survive.
events.revealBlurb: February 24, 1607 — Claudio Monteverdi at the court of the Gonzagas in Mantua. The orchestra called for some 40 instruments. The character of Orpheus was sung by tenor Francesco Rasi; the audience was tiny — members of the Accademia degli Invaghiti.

events.title: Kind of Blue Released
events.blurb: A 33-year-old trumpet player released a five-track album recorded in two half-day sessions in a converted Manhattan church. He had given the musicians — including a young tenor saxophonist he had just hired — only short modal sketches, not written music, and one of the tracks was a single take. The album would become the best-selling jazz record of all time, its influence extending to rock, classical minimalism, and film scoring.
events.revealBlurb: August 17, 1959 — Miles Davis at 30th Street Studio, NYC. Sidemen: John Coltrane, Cannonball Adderley, Bill Evans, Paul Chambers, Jimmy Cobb. It has sold over 5 million copies in the US alone, received quintuple-platinum status.

events.title: Beatles on Ed Sullivan
events.blurb: Four young British musicians from a northwestern English port city performed live on a Sunday-evening American variety show before an audience of 73 million viewers — at the time the largest in U.S. television history. The hysteria had preceded them: 7,000 people had mobbed their arrival at a New York airport two days earlier. Adult commentators dismissed them as a passing fad; younger Americans rearranged their evening to watch.
events.revealBlurb: February 9, 1964 — The Beatles at Studio 50, Manhattan. The crime rate during the broadcast was unusually low — even, it was said, in Times Square. They returned the next two Sundays for back-to-back appearances.

events.title: Bob Marley's Exodus Released
events.blurb: A Jamaican reggae star, recovering in a London flat after being shot in an assassination attempt at his home five months earlier, released his ninth studio album. Its tracks — "Three Little Birds," "One Love," "Jamming," "Waiting in Vain," and the title track — would become the core of his international legacy. Time magazine named it the album of the century. He had fled to London for his safety; the exile shaped the record.
events.revealBlurb: June 3, 1977 — Bob Marley and the Wailers. The album was recorded at Island Studios in London. The attempted assassination on December 3, 1976 had injured him, his wife, and his manager. Marley would die of cancer at 36 in 1981.

events.title: Nirvana's Nevermind Released
events.blurb: A three-piece rock band from the Pacific Northwest released their second album — recorded for $65,000, with a cover showing a naked infant underwater reaching for a dollar bill on a fishhook. The album's lead single had been written, according to the band, to sound "like the Pixies" and made a mockery of that idea. By January it had displaced Michael Jackson's "Dangerous" at number one and changed what major-label rock sounded like for the rest of the decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 24, 1991 — Nirvana, Kurt Cobain, Krist Novoselic, Dave Grohl. The lead single was "Smells Like Teen Spirit." The infant on the cover, Spencer Elden, later sued the band (unsuccessfully) for using his image.

events.title: First World Series
events.blurb: A best-of-nine championship series between the American League and National League pennant winners was played — the first time the two major leagues had agreed to a postseason championship after years of cold war. An underdog American League team, the Boston Americans, defeated the heavily favoured Pittsburgh Pirates 5 games to 3. The Pirates' owner, Barney Dreyfuss, had proposed the series himself.
events.revealBlurb: October 1-13, 1903 — Boston Americans (later the Red Sox) beat the Pittsburgh Pirates. Cy Young, Boston's 36-year-old ace, started game 3 but was the losing pitcher. Dreyfuss gave his losing Pirates a share of the winners' purse to compensate. No World Series was held in 1904; it became annual from 1905.

events.title: Babe Ruth's Called Shot
events.blurb: A Yankee slugger, facing a Cubs pitcher in game 3 of a World Series at a Chicago ballpark amid heckling from the dugout and the crowd, gestured with his bat toward the center field bleachers and then, on the next pitch, hit a home run that landed roughly where he had pointed. Whether he had actually "called" the shot is debated among eyewitnesses and film analysts to this day; teammates and opponents offered contradictory accounts for decades. The legend has long since outgrown the facts.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1932 — Babe Ruth at Wrigley Field. Opposing pitcher: Charlie Root, who denied the called shot to his death. An 8mm home movie shot by a Chicago fan, discovered in 1992, shows Ruth pointing — but whether to the outfield or the Cubs dugout is still contested.

events.title: Battle of the Sexes Tennis Match
events.blurb: A 29-year-old professional tennis player defeated a 55-year-old former Wimbledon champion in straight sets before a crowd of 30,000 at the Houston Astrodome and a television audience of 90 million. The retired player had publicly declared that no woman could defeat him, offering a $100,000 prize to any who tried.

events.title: Hank Aaron Breaks Ruth's Record
events.blurb: A 40-year-old Atlanta outfielder hit his 715th career home run off a Los Angeles Dodgers pitcher, breaking Babe Ruth's 39-year-old career record in front of a sellout home crowd. He had endured a year of death threats, racist mail, and FBI protection as he approached the record. As he rounded second base, two white college students ran onto the field alongside him — security later decided they had meant only to escort him. He tipped his cap as he crossed home plate.
events.revealBlurb: April 8, 1974 — Hank Aaron at Atlanta-Fulton County Stadium, off Al Downing. His final career total was 755 home runs, which stood as the record until Barry Bonds passed it in 2007. The FBI had warned him that multiple credible plots to assassinate him were active that season.

events.title: Kobe Bryant Dies
events.blurb: A 41-year-old retired basketball star, his 13-year-old daughter, and seven other passengers died when their private helicopter crashed into a hillside in thick fog outside Los Angeles while en route to a youth basketball game. The retired player had won five NBA championships, two Olympic golds, and the nickname "Black Mamba" during a 20-year career entirely with the Los Angeles Lakers. The crash prompted an outpouring of mourning around the world.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 2020 — Kobe and Gianna Bryant. National Transportation Safety Board findings attributed the crash to pilot error in poor visibility. His 2017 jersey-retirement ceremony at Staples Center saw both his numbers (8 and 24) raised to the rafters — the only player in franchise history with multiple retired numbers.

events.title: Pong Released in Arcades
events.blurb: A black-and-white rectangle containing two paddles and a bouncing dot was installed in a Sunnyvale, California tavern as a hardware test. The test machine broke within days — not from malfunction, but because the coin slot had overflowed with quarters. Atari scrambled to ship units nationwide, and the commercial video game industry was born.
events.revealBlurb: November 29, 1972 — Atari Inc., founded that June by Nolan Bushnell and Ted Dabney, shipped Pong to arcades. The Andy Capp's Tavern prototype jammed after a week because it held too many coins.

events.title: North American Video Game Crash
events.blurb: The home video game market had grown so fast that no one noticed it had filled up with garbage. Retailers were buried in unsold cartridges, consumers had lost all trust, and by 1985 an industry that had been worth $3.2 billion two years earlier had collapsed to $100 million — a 97 percent decline. Atari buried millions of unsold cartridges in a New Mexico landfill.
events.revealBlurb: 1983–1985 — Annual revenue fell from $3.2 billion (1983) to approximately $100 million (1985). The Atari landfill in Alamogordo, New Mexico — long an urban legend — was excavated in April 2014 and confirmed to contain millions of E.T. cartridges.

events.title: Half-Life Released by Valve
events.blurb: Every first-person shooter before Half-Life presented missions as separate levels with loading screens and no coherent world. Half-Life placed the player inside a continuous unbroken environment, told its story entirely through actions the player participated in, and won more than 50 Game of the Year awards. Critics later divided gaming history into "pre-Half-Life" and "post-Half-Life" eras.
events.revealBlurb: November 19, 1998 — Valve's debut game released for Windows. Budgeted for lifetime sales of 180,000 copies, it sold 212,000 in the United States alone by year-end and ultimately over 9 million copies. It spawned Counter-Strike as a fan mod. Valve used the revenue to build Steam.

events.title: Counter-Strike Released as Standalone
events.blurb: Two amateur developers built a modification for Half-Life in which terrorists and counter-terrorists fought in small tactical maps. Valve noticed the mod's download numbers, purchased the rights, and released it as a standalone product. It became the most-played online game in the world for over a decade, the game credited with institutionalising competitive PC gaming.
events.revealBlurb: November 9, 2000 — Counter-Strike version 1.0 released as a free Half-Life modification. Creators Minh "Gooseman" Le and Jess Cliffe had started the mod in June 1999. In 2023, CS:GO/CS2 peaked at over 1.8 million concurrent Steam players.

events.title: Fortnite Battle Royale Mode Launches
events.blurb: Epic released a free-to-play mode in which 100 players parachuted onto an island and fought until one survived, funded entirely by cosmetic purchases. Within two months it had more players than any game in history. It didn't invent the battle royale genre, but it perfected the business model — and convinced the rest of the industry that free-to-play with optional cosmetics was the future.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 2017 — Fortnite Battle Royale launched free on PC, PlayStation 4, and Xbox One. Within two months it had 45 million players. The game's in-game concerts — including Travis Scott's 2020 event with 12.3 million simultaneous viewers — redefined live entertainment.

events.title: Stockton & Darlington Railway Opens
events.blurb: A steam locomotive hauling 21 coal wagons and one passenger coach completed a 40-kilometre journey through County Durham at a top speed of 24 km/h, carrying 450 passengers on its inaugural run. It was the first railway to carry both freight and fare-paying passengers using steam traction.

events.title: Transatlantic Telegraph Cable Completed
events.blurb: The steamship Great Eastern finished laying 4,000 kilometres of insulated copper wire across the floor of the Atlantic, connecting Valencia Island, Ireland, to Heart's Content, Newfoundland. The first commercial message crossed in minutes — a journey that had previously taken ten days by ship.

events.title: Edison Invents Phonograph
events.blurb: A 30-year-old American inventor shouted the first verse of "Mary Had a Little Lamb" into the horn of a machine he had built at his New Jersey laboratory, then cranked a handle to make the machine play his words back to him. Recording sound — not just transmitting it instantaneously as the telephone did — had never been done before. The device, a tinfoil-cylinder phonograph, would be followed by commercial wax-cylinder versions by the end of the decade.
events.revealBlurb: November 21, 1877 — Thomas Edison at Menlo Park. The original tinfoil phonograph could replay a recording only a few times before the foil wore out. The machine astonished audiences when Edison demonstrated it at the Scientific American office a week later.

events.title: Eiffel Tower Opens
events.blurb: A 300-metre wrought-iron lattice tower, built over two years, two months, and five days as the entrance arch to a Paris world's fair, was completed. At three times the height of the Washington Monument, it was the tallest man-made structure in the world and would remain so for 41 years. A petition signed by 300 prominent French artists had protested the "useless and monstrous" project during construction. It was intended to be demolished after 20 years; radio antennas saved it.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1889 — designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centennial of the French Revolution. It remained the tallest building until the 1930 Chrysler Building. The Nazi occupation cut the elevator cables; Parisians said the "Hitler had to climb the stairs to the top."

events.title: Ford Model T Goes on Sale
events.blurb: An American automaker released a new car designed to be cheap, simple to drive, and reliable on the rutted rural roads of the era. It sold for $850 — about half the price of the cheapest competitor. Over 19 years of production, the company would build 15 million of them, mostly painted black because that paint dried fastest. At peak production, a completed Model T rolled off the line every 24 seconds.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1908 — Ford Motor Company. The 1913-1914 introduction of the moving assembly line cut the Model T's price to $490. Henry Ford doubled the minimum wage at his Highland Park plant to $5 a day in January 1914, partly to cut turnover caused by the line's brutal monotony.

events.title: Hippocratic Oath Composed
events.blurb: Greek medical writers associated with a physician teaching on an Aegean island composed a short ethical oath addressed to Apollo and Asclepius, binding physicians to care for their patients, respect their teachers, preserve patient confidences, and do no harm. The document is arguably the oldest surviving code of professional ethics. Modern versions, substantially modified, are still sworn by many medical-school graduates.
events.revealBlurb: c. 400 BCE — attributed to Hippocrates of Kos, though probably composed by his students or school. The modern "first, do no harm" is actually not in the original Greek text; it appears later in Hippocrates' Epidemics. The oath still shows up at white-coat ceremonies.

events.title: Fleming Discovers Penicillin
events.blurb: A 47-year-old Scottish bacteriologist returning from a summer holiday to his London laboratory noticed that one of the staphylococcus-culture plates he had left stacked on his bench had been contaminated by a mold, and that a clear zone of inhibition around the mold showed the bacteria had died there. He identified the mold genus, isolated an anti-bacterial substance it produced, and published his findings — which were largely ignored for over a decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 28, 1928 — Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford successfully purified penicillin in 1941, making it a usable drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel with Fleming. The drug's mass production during WWII saved hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives.

events.title: First Human Heart Transplant
events.blurb: A South African surgeon transplanted the heart of a 25-year-old accident victim into a 53-year-old grocer in a nine-hour operation at Groote Schuur Hospital in Cape Town. The recipient survived 18 days before dying of pneumonia; the same surgical team performed a second transplant 13 days later — that patient lived 19 months.

events.title: First CT Scanner
events.blurb: A British engineer at a small electronics company introduced the first clinical computed tomography scanner, which used X-ray beams and computer reconstruction to produce cross-sectional images of the inside of a patient — the first medical imaging breakthrough since the X-ray 76 years earlier. Early scans took hours and resolved only the head; within a decade the technology could produce full-body scans in minutes.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1971 — Godfrey Hounsfield at EMI; first clinical scan at Atkinson Morley's Hospital, Wimbledon, London. Hounsfield shared the 1979 Nobel with Allan Cormack. EMI funded the research from its Beatles albums revenue.

events.title: Human Genome Draft Published
events.blurb: Two groups — the international Human Genome Project consortium and the private company Celera Genomics, which had entered the race late with a competing methodology — simultaneously published their draft sequences of the 3 billion base pairs of the human genome in the journals Nature and Science. The entries were the culmination of 11 years of work and a vast investment of computing and laboratory resources. Humans had roughly 21,000 genes — far fewer than most biologists had predicted.
events.revealBlurb: February 12, 2001 — publications in Nature (consortium) and Science (Celera). The "finished" version of the sequence arrived in 2003. Sequencing a human genome now costs about $200 (down from $2.7 billion) and takes a day.

events.title: Munich Agreement
events.blurb: Four heads of government met through the night in a grand hall in southern Europe and handed over a democratic nation's border region to an aggressive neighbour — without inviting a single representative of that nation to the table. The leader who returned home waving the signed paper declared it meant peace; within six months the entire country had been swallowed.
events.revealBlurb: September 30, 1938 — Chamberlain, Daladier, Hitler, and Mussolini signed over the Sudetenland at 1:30 AM. Chamberlain's "peace for our time" paper became history's most mocked diplomatic document. Czechoslovakia's envoys waited in an anteroom and were simply informed of the result.

events.title: Fall of France
events.blurb: German armoured divisions crossed a forested highland deemed impassable by military doctrine, bypassed the most elaborate fixed defences in Europe, and in six weeks forced the capitulation of a nation whose army was considered the strongest on the continent. An armistice was signed in the same railway carriage used for the previous war's peace.
events.revealBlurb: May 10 – June 22, 1940. The armistice was signed at Compiègne in Hitler's deliberate reversal of the 1918 Armistice humiliation — he had the original railway carriage brought out of a museum. France lost 92,000 killed in six weeks. A junior general named de Gaulle flew to London and refused to accept the result.

events.title: Rosie the Riveter Campaign
events.blurb: A deliberate government and industry campaign to recruit women into heavy industrial and weapons manufacturing work portrayed a bandana-wearing figure flexing her arm above the slogan "We Can Do It!" alongside magazine illustrations that reached millions of households, reshaping public expectations of gender and labour across a nation at industrial-scale mobilisation.
events.revealBlurb: 1942–1943. The number of women in the US workforce rose from 12 million to 20 million — a 57% increase — by 1944. Women built B-29s, welded Liberty ships, and operated cranes. The Westinghouse "We Can Do It!" poster was seen by almost no one during the war; it was rediscovered in the 1980s and became an icon of the feminist movement.

events.title: Fall of Monte Cassino
events.blurb: After four separate offensives spanning five months, Polish troops raised their flag over the ruins of a hilltop monastery that had been reduced to rubble by an Allied bombing raid — finally cracking a mountain defensive line that had blocked the Allied advance up a peninsula for half a year and cost over 43,000 casualties across all the assaulting armies.
events.revealBlurb: May 18, 1944. Polish Corps commander General Anders had promised his men they would fight for Poland in the west since the Soviet Union had taken the east. Over 900 Polish soldiers died in the final assault. The monastery's Benedictine monks had evacuated its art treasures months earlier; the abbey itself was empty during the famous Allied bombing of February 15.

events.title: Nuremberg Verdicts
events.blurb: An international tribunal delivered verdicts against 22 senior leaders of a defeated regime after ten months of proceedings that introduced "crimes against humanity" as a concept in international law — finding twelve guilty of offences for which they would be executed, and establishing the principle that following government orders is not a defence against such charges.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1946. Hermann Göring cheated the hangman by swallowing a cyanide capsule hours before his scheduled execution — a capsule no one ever satisfactorily explained. The other ten were hanged on October 16. Three defendants were acquitted. The tribunal's procedural framework became the model for every subsequent international war crimes court.

events.title: First Networked Email
events.blurb: A computer engineer working for a Cambridge, Massachusetts research firm sent an electronic message between two computers sitting next to each other in his office, using a symbol from the typewriter keyboard he'd picked precisely because it was never used in names — the "at" sign — to separate the user name from the host machine name. He could not recall years later what the message had contained; probably "QWERTYUIOP" or similar.
events.revealBlurb: October 1971 — Ray Tomlinson at BBN Technologies. The @ symbol's adoption was arbitrary but lasting. Tomlinson's contribution is the reason your email address contains an @. He died in 2016.

events.title: Facebook Launched
events.blurb: A 19-year-old Harvard sophomore with a history of making unauthorized student-directory sites launched, from his dorm room, a social network restricted to students with harvard.edu email addresses. It reached half the Harvard student body within two weeks. He expanded to Yale, Columbia, and Stanford within weeks. Within a year he had dropped out; within four he was a billionaire on paper.
events.revealBlurb: February 4, 2004 — Mark Zuckerberg at Harvard, with co-founders Eduardo Saverin, Andrew McCollum, Dustin Moskovitz, and Chris Hughes. Originally thefacebook.com. Zuckerberg settled with the Winklevoss twins for $65 million in 2008; they spent it on Bitcoin.

events.title: Airbnb Founded
events.blurb: Three San Francisco roommates, unable to pay rent, inflated three air mattresses in their loft and rented them to attendees of a design conference who could not find hotel rooms. They built a website for the arrangement, expanded to renting other people's spare rooms, and were nearly rejected by Y Combinator before the program accepted them in early 2009. The company would be valued at $100 billion at its 2020 IPO.
events.revealBlurb: August 11, 2008 — Brian Chesky, Joe Gebbia, Nathan Blecharczyk. They funded early growth by selling novelty political cereals — Obama O's and Cap'n McCain's — at the 2008 Democratic and Republican conventions.

events.title: Instagram Launched
events.blurb: A two-person startup released a free iOS app that let users take photos, apply one of eleven retro filters, and share them to a simple timeline-based social network. It acquired 25,000 users on launch day and its first million within three months. Facebook bought the company for $1 billion in cash and stock eighteen months later, when it had thirteen employees and zero revenue.
events.revealBlurb: October 6, 2010 — Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger. Originally built as a location-based check-in app called Burbn. The $1 billion Facebook acquisition in April 2012 is now considered one of the great bargains in tech history.

events.title: Snapchat Launched
events.blurb: Three Stanford undergraduates released an iOS app that let users send photos that automatically disappeared a few seconds after being viewed. One founder had pitched the idea for a product-design class the previous spring and been told it was terrible. The app would grow explosively as a teenage-first social platform and introduce "Stories," a format quickly copied by every major competitor.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 2011 — Evan Spiegel, Bobby Murphy, and Reggie Brown. Originally named Picaboo. Facebook offered to acquire Snap for $3 billion in 2013; Spiegel said no. Snap went public in 2017 at a $24 billion valuation.
